title: Feedbacks in Earth Systems
seo_title: Earth Systems Worksheets: Feedback Loops, Albedo and Sea-Ice Data (High School Earth Science)
standard_text: Analyze geoscience data to make the claim that one change to Earth's surface can create feedbacks that cause changes to other Earth systems.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on feedbacks in Earth systems (NGSS HS-ESS2-2): Earth's spheres, positive and negative feedback, albedo and sea-ice data. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: One change can trigger many more.
key_sub: Positive feedbacks amplify a change; negative feedbacks dampen it.
body_html:
How to think about it

A change in one Earth system can set off feedbacks in others.

  • Systems: geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere.
  • Positive feedback amplifies a change (melting ice → darker surface → more warming). Negative feedback reduces it.
  • Albedo: fraction of sunlight reflected. Absorbed = incoming × (1 − albedo).
Example

Albedo 6%, sunlight 400 W/m². Absorbed?

400 × 0.94

Answer: 376 W/m²

Example

Permafrost thaws, releasing methane, more warming. Type?

The change grows

Answer: positive feedback

Common mistakes

  • Thinking positive feedback means a good result.
  • Thinking a change stays in one sphere.
  • Thinking dark surfaces reflect more sunlight.

faq.q: What is the difference between positive and negative feedback?
faq.a: Positive feedback makes a change grow larger. Negative feedback makes a change smaller and helps keep a system stable.
Warming melts ice, exposing darker land or ocean that absorbs more sunlight, which causes more warming and more melting.

faq.q: How can one change affect other Earth systems?
faq.a: For example, a volcano (geosphere) adds particles to the atmosphere that cool the climate, which can affect ice, oceans and living things.

items.q: Why does melting snow speed up warming?
c: Darker ground underneath absorbs more sunlight.
items.e: Lower albedo.

items.q: More CO₂ helps some plants grow faster, and they take more CO₂ out of the air. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Sunlight of 200 W/m² falls on open ocean (albedo 6%). How much energy is absorbed per square meter?
Why did global temperatures drop after the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption?
c: Sulfur gases made particles that reflected sunlight.
items.e: Geosphere → atmosphere.

items.q: Warming melts sea ice, exposing dark ocean that absorbs more sunlight, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: A city paves over a large area. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Which absorbs more sunlight: cropland (albedo 20%) or sea ice (albedo 60%)?
items.e: Lower albedo → less reflected → more absorbed.

items.q: What does a negative feedback do?
c: It reduces the change and helps keep a system stable.
items.e: Stabilizing.

items.q: A hotter Earth gives off more infrared energy to space, which cools it down. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: How can cutting a forest change the atmosphere?
c: It has no effect on air.
Fewer trees take in CO₂, and burning or decay releases more CO₂.
items.e: Biosphere → atmosphere.

items.q: What are Earth's main systems (spheres)?
c: geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere and cryosphere
items.e: Interacting systems.

items.q: A volcano erupts and puts ash and gases high into the sky. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Warmer air holds more water vapor, a greenhouse gas, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Does 'positive feedback' mean the result is good?
c: No. It means the change gets bigger.
items.e: Amplifying.

items.q: What is a feedback loop?
c: a change that causes effects that then increase or decrease the original change
items.e: Loops.

items.q: What is albedo?
c: the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects
items.e: Snow is high, ocean is low.

items.q: Wildfires burn forests, releasing CO₂ that warms the climate and dries more forests. What kind of feedback is this?

the geosphere and hydrosphere (coasts erode faster without reefs)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.
